Why do I get the impression that there is far too little discussion of the proposal for a regulation on combatting online child sexual abuse material?

I am referring to the ‘Chat Control’ (or CSAM) EU Commission's Regulation proposal which, in my opinion, raises grave concerns about the respect of fundamental rights (including privacy and data protection) in the EU, also undermining security in the digital world.

This proposal envisages mass scanning of private communications, including encrypted conversations, raising serious issues of compliance with Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights by threatening to undermine the data security of citizens, businesses and institutions in the EU. 

The CSAM Regulation proposal deals with a mandatory weakening of end-to-end encryption - something that would be able to create security gaps open to exploitation by cybercriminals, terrorist organisations, and would also harm the competitiveness of the EU digital economy.

The proposed technical approach is based on automated content analysis tools, potentially able to produce high rates of false positives, and therefore creating the risk that innocent users could be wrongly incriminated, while the effectiveness of this approach in protecting children has not been proven.

But the EU Parliament and the Council have repeatedly rejected mass surveillance (e.g., facial recognition in public spaces).

So, are we sure that child protection is achieved through the measures referred to in the Chat Control Regulation proposal, without violating the fundamental rights of EU citizens? And what about the negative impact on cybersecurity and economic competitiveness caused by weakening encryption?

body:
The EU's "Chat Control" proposal, formally the Regulation on the Prevention and Combating of Child Sexual Abuse, aims to mandate client-side scanning of private digital communications - including messages, photos, and videos on users' devices before encryption. This would involve tools like hash matching against known child sexual abuse material (CSAM) databases, machine learning for detecting new content, and URL checks, potentially requiring backdoors in apps and operating systems. While framed as child protection, critics argue it enables mass surveillance, violates privacy rights under EU law (e.g., Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights), and conflicts with European Court of Justice rulings against blanket monitoring.
As of October 12, 2025, the proposal is advancing under the Danish Presidency of the EU Council, with a key vote scheduled for October 14. Nine member states oppose it, 12 support, and six (including Germany) remain undecided. Germany's recent firm opposition - citing risks to confidential communications - has dealt a significant blow, potentially stalling progress. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and the EU Council's Legal Service have flagged human rights and legality concerns. If passed, scanning could begin as early as late 2025, affecting 450 million EU citizens and services like Signal, WhatsApp, and email providers.
Risks include weakening end-to-end encryption (E2EE), creating exploitable vulnerabilities for hackers or abusers, false positives (e.g., flagging innocent family photos), and mission creep to scan other content like political speech. Politicians, police, and military may be exempt under "professional secrecy" rules.

The intent behind the proposed EU Chat Control proposal is noble, yet we must tread carefully to avoid eroding the very freedom and privacy we aim to protect.

The regulation’s idea of scanning every message, photo, and video on every device, even before they are sent, shifts the paradigm from targeted investigation to mass surveillance. 

Its execution is also expected to be difficult as automated detection systems, even when built with the best intentions, are prone to error and a false positive in such a sensitive domain can impact reputations, careers, and lives.

The other challenge is in the nature of CSAM - in which context matters as much as content. What appears to be a medical image in one setting could be misinterpreted in another. 

While child protection is a societal responsibility, turning a smartphone into a surveillance device may not yield the expected outcome. Instead, the solution lies in training and enabling law enforcement, educators, and the investigators and provide them with latest tools to investigate the incidents.

In this cyber world, we have an uncomfortable question to answer - do we invest in tech and tools for monitoring the incidents, or invest in human capability to discern, investigate, and respond with judgment and empathy?

Longread: why I am against the commission proposal for chat control. In short, it is not a solution for child abuse but does form a serious threat to our privacy. The long answer 👇 

The European Commission wants WhatsApp, Signal, and other messaging services to scan your private messages in real-time. This is a direct threat to every citizen's digital privacy.

What's at stake?
Under the guise of fighting child sexual abuse material (CSAM), the Commission proposes mass surveillance of all private communications. The intention may be noble, but the means are fundamentally flawed and dangerous.

Why this proposal must be stopped?
1. Your privacy is under attack: The proposal undermines end-to-end encryption—the digital equivalent of your private home. Encryption isn't about hiding wrongdoing; it's about living securely in a digital world without constant scrutiny.
2. Function creep risk: Technology designed to detect child abuse images today could be repurposed by authoritarian regimes to hunt political opponents tomorrow. In our current global context, this isn't far-fetched.
3. Ineffective by design: Criminals adapt quickly. They'll simply migrate to unregulated apps and private networks, while millions of law-abiding citizens lose their privacy and security.

Our alternative
Our Green group, along with the broader Parliament, has consistently opposed mass surveillance from day one. Instead, we've proposed a three-pillar approach that's both more effective and privacy-respecting:
1. Security by design: Apps must be built safely from the ground up—with blocking/reporting functions, user consent for sharing contact details, and moderation of high-risk public chats.
2. Targeted action: The new EU Child Protection Centre should automatically search publicly accessible content (including the dark web) for known CSAM—far more effective than surveilling private messages.
3. Swift removal: Providers must remove clearly illegal material immediately—unlike the Commission's proposal which focuses on surveillance rather than action. 

The bottom line
Mass surveillance isn't the answer to protecting children online. We can fight CSAM effectively without sacrificing everyone's fundamental right to privacy.
Child welfare is paramount—that's exactly why we support the new directive to combat child abuse, which Parliament adopted with near-unanimous support. But we can protect children without creating a surveillance state.

Europe is about to make a choice that could redefine digital privacy

There's a vote coming up on October 14th that deserves more attention than it's getting. 
The EU's proposed Child Sexual Abuse Regulation—nicknamed "Chat Control"—would require messaging platforms to scan private messages, including encrypted ones, for child abuse material.
The stated goal is obviously important: protecting children. But the method? That's where things get complicated.

What's happening right now:
Germany, Belgium, Italy, and Sweden—countries that previously supported mandatory scanning—are now wavering. They're listed as "undecided." Still, at least 12 EU member states are backing the proposal.

Over 500 scientists have signed open letters opposing it. 
Their concern? You can't scan end-to-end encrypted messages without fundamentally breaking encryption. 
And once you break it for one purpose, you've broken it for everything.
Why this should matter to anyone building or securing digital systems:
Encryption isn't just a nice-to-have—it's the foundation of secure communication. 
Medical records, financial transactions, whistleblower communications, trade secrets—all of it depends on the guarantee that encrypted means actually encrypted.

If Chat Control passes, we're looking at:
Precedent creep. 
Today it's CSAM. Tomorrow it could be "terrorism." Next year, "misinformation." The technical capability, once built, doesn't go away.

Regulatory chaos. 
Companies will face conflicting mandates across jurisdictions. The EU says scan. Other regions say don't you dare weaken encryption. Good luck operating globally.

Trust collapse. 
Users in sensitive fields—healthcare, finance, journalism—will abandon platforms that can't guarantee privacy. And they should.

What we should be doing:
If you're building products, double down on privacy-by-design. If you're in leadership, get involved in these policy debates—lawmakers need to hear from people who actually understand how this technology works.

We need to prepare for a fragmented regulatory landscape. Build compliance flexibility into your systems. Be transparent with users about what you do and don't scan, and why.

The hard question:
Is there actually a middle ground here? 
Can we protect vulnerable children without dismantling the privacy infrastructure that protects everyone else? Or are we being forced into a false choice?

I'm genuinely curious: what's your take? 
How should companies respond when governments demand access to encrypted communications for any reason, however well-intentioned?
Because this vote isn't just about one regulation. It's about what kind of internet we're building.

Day 5 of posting an argument (almost) every day why the Chat Control proposal should be dropped. Here we go:

After the post about false positives in broad terms (https://lnkd.in/dr3_cX4S), today I want write a bit about what these false positives would be, and why they are definitely an important data protection problem. 

It would be bad enough if images sent over, say, WhatsApp would be falsely flagged as CSAM at random with a small probability. This is not, however, how the classifying algorithms would behave. They would, of course, mistake images for CSAM more likely if they are more similar to CSAM. This means while a photo of an excavator would probably be pretty safe from erroneously being reported to the police, some very personal photos would have a much higher risk of being reported.

I find the thought of personal photos having a small chance of being sent to the police extremely chilling. But even if you think you would be fine with this, I'd like you to consider two additional points. Firstly, you are probably thinking of your police in your country, but there is nothing in the proposal that provides limits which police authorities this data can be shared with. And secondly, there are probably people who have more and more powerful enemies than you have. As an example, consider a volunteer who does fundraising for some Ukrainian organization. I would understand if this person did not want to share their personal images with the police authority of certain EU member states.

Better known by its moniker, #ChatControl, the proposal aims to compel #tech companies to scan all private #digital communications — including #encrypted #chats and #emails — for child #sexualabuse material (#CSAM) and #grooming behaviours. 
While its objective is laudable, the proposed method of client-side #scanning is divisive and redefines the role of #cybersecurity professionals. 
The political 🇪🇺 landscape is deeply split, with the fate of the regulation hanging in the balance. As of September 2025, the outcome of the upcoming vote remains highly unpredictable. Austria, Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, the Czech Republic, and Finland oppose it.

This political schism highlights a fundamental clash of values. However, beyond the corridors of Brussels, the regulation poses a profound, perhaps existential, crisis for the cybersecurity profession. If passed, it would force a paradigm shift, moving the role of a security expert from protector to overseer
🔎It is an ethical and professional crossroads. The impact on cybersecurity professionals can be distilled into two critical areas:
1️⃣ Ethical conflict and legal liability: the regulation would legally compel software engineers and security experts to design and implement systems that inherently weaken security and create vulnerabilities. 
➡️ This stands in direct opposition to the core #ethical tenets of their profession, which mandate the duty to protect data, infrastructure, and society. Professionals would be caught in the paradox of having to build insecurity into systems to comply with the law, creating an irreconcilable conflict with codes of conduct from bodies like the ISC2.
2️⃣ The rise of surveillance compliance: the law would likely spawn a new, and arguably perverse, area of specialisation — surveillance compliance. 
➡️ The focus for many cyber and security teams would inevitably shift from defending against external threats to implementing and maintaining internal monitoring mechanisms.
This fundamentally alters the professional's role from being a guardian of the user and their data to an enabler of state-mandated surveillance, eroding the trust that underpins the entire digital ecosystem. The EU’s Chat Control 2.0 proposal seeks to mandate the scanning of all private digital communications—messages, emails, cloud files—even those secured with end-to-end encryption, in order to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM). While intended to protect children, it effectively establishes mass suspicionless surveillance of EU citizens.

Key risks:

- Privacy violations: All messages are scanned without a warrant, undermining the right to confidential correspondence and anonymous communication.

- Encryption backdoors: Client-side scanning destroys secure encryption, exposing data to hackers, criminals, and foreign intelligence.

- False positives: Evidence from Switzerland and Ireland shows up to 80% of reports are irrelevant, overwhelming police with noise and diverting resources from real cases.

- Wrong targets: Organized abusers avoid mainstream platforms, while teenagers’ consensual sexting is often criminalized.

- Democratic erosion: Creates a surveillance infrastructure easily repurposed for censorship, copyright policing, or silencing dissent.


Legal and political concerns:

- Experts and former ECJ judges warn the proposal is disproportionate and unlikely to withstand judicial review.

- Over 72% of EU citizens oppose mandatory chat scanning; 500+ scientists call it technically infeasible.

- Providers like Signal and Threema threaten to exit the EU market rather than compromise encryption.


Alternatives exist:

 - Targeted, warrant-based surveillance of suspects.

- Mandatory removal of known CSAM from hosting services.

- Strengthened police units, cross-border cooperation, and undercover investigations.

- Education, media literacy, and robust victim support.


Conclusion: Chat Control 2.0 risks harming victims more than helping them—criminalizing minors, destroying safe spaces, and weakening Europe’s cybersecurity. Protecting children must not come at the cost of mass surveillance and loss of digital freedom.

Schrödinger's Crime: AI-generated Child Sexual Abuse Material as a Victimless Offense (2024):
" The emergence of fully AI-generated Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) presents a novel and complex challenge to European Union (EU) legal frameworks. This thesis critically examines the adequacy of existing and proposed EU legislation in addressing AI-generated CSAM, with a focus on the 2024 Proposal for a Revised Directive on combating child sexual abuse. By analyzing the legal definitions of CSAM, the principle of harm, and the discretion afforded to EU Member States in criminalizing virtual CSAM, the study evaluates the implications of treating fully AI-generated CSAM as a criminal offense. Key challenges include the absence of direct victims, difficulties in distinguishing AI-generated content from real imagery, and the risks of overcriminalization. Through a doctrinal analysis of legal principles and legislative texts, this thesis seeks to clarify whether the criminalization of fully AI-generated CSAM can be justified within the boundaries of established EU legal norms, while also addressing practical enforcement concerns. The research concludes with recommendations on harmonizing EU laws to effectively regulate this emerging issue. "

Resistance to Hungarian presidency’s new push for child sexual abuse prevention regulation - because it's a draconian spying law asking for 100% coverage of digital comms - Resistance to the Hungarian presidency’s approach to the EU’s draft law to combat online child sexual abuse material (CSAM) was still palpable during a member states’ meeting on Wednesday (4 September).

The Hungarian presidency of the Council of the EU aims to secure consensus on the proposed law to combat online child sexual abuse material (CSAM) by October, according to an EU diplomat and earlier reports by Politico.

Hungary has prepared a compromise note on the draft law, also reported by Contexte.

The note, presented at a meeting of ambassadors on Wednesday, seeks political guidance to make progress at the technical level, the EU diplomat told Euractiv.

With the voluntary regime expiring in mid-2026, most member states agree that urgent action is needed, the diplomat continued.

But some member states are still resistant to the Hungarian’s latest approach.

The draft law to detect and remove online child sexual abuse material (CSAM) was removed from the agenda of Thursday’s (20 June) meeting of the Committee of Permanent Representatives (COREPER), who were supposed to vote on it.

Sources close to the matter told Euractiv, that Poland and Germany remain opposed to the proposal, with smaller member states also voicing concerns, potentially forming a blocking minority.

Although France and the Netherlands initially supported the proposal, the Netherlands has since withdrawn its support, and Italy has indicated that the new proposal is moving in the right direction.

As a result, no agreement was reached to move forward.

Currently, an interim regulation allows companies to voluntarily detect and report online CSAM. Originally set to expire in 2024, this measure has been extended to 2026 to avoid a legislative gap, as the draft for a permanent law has yet to be agreed.

Hungary is expected to introduce a concrete textual proposal soon. The goal is to agree on its general approach by October, the EU diplomat said, a fully agreed position among member states which serves as the basis for negotiations with the European Parliament.

Meanwhile, the European Commission is preparing to send a detailed opinion to Hungary regarding the draft law, expected by 30 September, Contexte reported on Wednesday.

In the text, the presidency also suggested extending the temporary exemption from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive, which governs privacy and electronic communications, for new CSAM and grooming.

Denmark currently holds the Presidency of the Council of the European Union. In this capacity, the Danish government has (re)submitted a proposal for a regulation aimed at preventing and combating child sexual abuse (Regulation to Prevent and Combat Child Sexual Abuse – CSAR), commonly referred to as “Chat Control”. 

In an op-ed published in Altinget.dk, Carsten Baum and Diego F. Aranha, strongly warn against the proposal:

“If European lawmakers approve the proposal, CSAR will require that large portions of digital communication within the EU — including all your images and videos — may potentially be scanned by state-installed surveillance software.

Authorities will automatically be notified of any communication detected as potentially containing Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM).”

This criticism follows in the wake of protests from over 400 experts in information security and privacy, who have opposed similar proposals put forward by previous presidencies.

According to the experts, CSAR is ineffective, dangerous, and represents a slippery slope towards an authoritarian surveillance society — one in which governments or presidents could easily begin scanning for other types of content they suddenly deem “dangerous”.

“There is no question that child sexual abuse and exploitation are heinous crimes that affect the most vulnerable among us,” write Baum and Aranha.

 “While child exploitation must be combated, it is crucial that the method be proportionate to the problem. We do not believe this is the case when mass real-time surveillance of ordinary citizens’ communications is introduced 
without any suspicion or charge.”

An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: AI-generated imagery and other forms of deepfakes depicting child sexual abuse (CSA) could be criminalized in the European Union under plans to update existing legislation to keep pace with technology developments, the Commission announced today. It's also proposing to create a new criminal offense of livestreaming child sexual abuse. The possession and exchange of "pedophile manuals" would also be criminalized under the plan -- which is part of a wider package of measures the EU says is intended to boost prevention of CSA, including by increasing awareness of online risks and to make it easier for victims to report crimes and obtain support (including granting them a right to financial compensation). The proposal to update the EU's current rules in this area, which date back to 2011, also includes changes around mandatory reporting of offenses.

Back in May 2022, the Commission presented a separate piece of CSA-related draft legislation, aiming to establish a framework that could make it obligatory for digital services to use automated technologies to detect and report existing or new child sexual abuse material (CSAM) circulating on their platforms, and identify and report grooming activity targeting kids. The CSAM-scanning plan has proven to be highly controversial -- and it continues to split lawmakers in the parliament and the Council, as well as kicking up suspicions over the Commission's links with child safety tech lobbyists and raising other awkward questions for the EU's executive, over a legally questionable foray into microtargeted ads to promote the proposal. The Commission's decision to prioritize the targeting of digital messaging platforms to tackle CSA has attracted a lot of criticism that the bloc's lawmakers are focusing in the wrong area for combatting a complex societal problem -- which may have generated some pressure for it to come with follow-on proposals. (Not that the Commission is saying that, of course; it describes today's package as "complementary" to its earlier CSAM-scanning proposal.) Against this background, on 30 November 2023, the Commission unveiled the proposal to extend the ePrivacy interim Regulation. 
 
Even though the Commission tried to avoid taking this measure at all costs, the difficulties experienced by the co-legislators, and in particular the Council, to reach an agreement on the long-term legislation proposed by the Commission in May 2022, have forced the EU Executive to find an alternative. The co-legislators though are not the only EU institutions to be blamed for not meeting the deadline. It should also be reminded that the Commission repeatedly delayed the presentation of the CSAM proposal while knowing that it was time-sensitive.
 
The Commission´s initiative consists of extending the ePrivacy interim Regulation which enables internet-based communications services to continue detecting and removing CSAM online on a voluntary basis for two more years, until 3 August 2026.
 
The ePrivacy interim Regulation establishes a derogation from Articles 5(1) and 6(1) of Directive 2002/58/EC (the ePrivacy Directive) which “𝑠ℎ𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑛𝑜𝑡 𝑎𝑝𝑝𝑙𝑦 𝑡𝑜 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑑𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝑜𝑓 𝑐𝑜𝑚𝑚𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑣𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑐𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑏𝑦 𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑣𝑖𝑑𝑒𝑟𝑠 𝑜𝑓 𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑠𝑜𝑛𝑎𝑙 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑜𝑡ℎ𝑒𝑟 𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎”. It applies to certain number-independent interpersonal communications services, without prejudice to their obligations under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
 
The proposal will be adopted by the co-legislators following the ordinary legislative procedure, which, in some cases has been concluded within four months. One example would be the 𝑅𝑒𝑔𝑢𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑎𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑓𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑒𝑤𝑜𝑟𝑘 𝑓𝑜𝑟 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑢𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒, 𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑖𝑓𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑎𝑐𝑐𝑒𝑝𝑡𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒 𝑜𝑓 𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑜𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑏𝑙𝑒 𝐶𝑂𝑉𝐼𝐷-19 𝑣𝑎𝑐𝑐𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛, 𝑡𝑒𝑠𝑡 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑦 𝑐𝑒𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑓𝑖𝑐𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠 𝑡𝑜 𝑓𝑎𝑐𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑒 𝑚𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑑𝑢𝑟𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑡ℎ𝑒 𝐶𝑂𝑉𝐼𝐷-19 𝑝𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑒𝑚𝑖𝑐 (´the EU Digital COVID Certificate Regulation extension´). ‘Let yourself be monitored’: EU governments to agree on Chat Control with user “consent” [updated]
European Parliament Freedom, democracy and transparency Press releases
Based on a new proposal by the Belgian Minister of the Interior, EU governments could endorse the much-criticised child sexual abuse regulation (CSAR or chat control) as early as June after all. This is what internal information leaked to Pirate Party MEP and shadow rapporteur Patrick Breyer reveals.
Specifically, according to the proposal, users of apps with a communication function would have to agree via terms and conditions or pop-up messages that all images and videos sent to others will be scanned automatically and possibly reported to the EU and the police. To this end, monitoring backdoors would need to be integrated into previously securely end-to-end encrypted messenger services, even though the Belgians claim that their proposed ‘upload moderation’ scheme differs from the much criticised ‘client-side scanning’. If a user does not agree to the scanning of their private photos and videos, they would still be able to use the service for sending text messages, but would no longer be able to share images and videos. The scanner algorithms are supposed to report known CSAM as well as unknown images and videos that are deemed potentially suspicious by ‘artificial intelligence’ technology. The scanning of text messages for indications of grooming, which has hardly been used to date, would be removed from the draft legislation, as would the scanning of audio communication, which is not in use at all.

More than 300 scientists from 33 countries have signed another open letter https://lnkd.in/e2W-iaxg criticising the latest EU #chatcontrol draft. The letter reconfirms 2 earlier letters from July 2023 https://lnkd.in/eTxh-CYn and May 2024 https://lnkd.in/eeP7uZC9

It was great to work again with Carmela Troncoso and the other team members. 

TLDR; The #chatcontrol proposal has been tweaked but it remains unacceptable: the solution does not work, undermines end-to-end encryption, is indiscriminate, leads to function creep and abuse by dictators and undermines the security of devices, apps, and the current techniques to detect illegal content. 

The latest proposal forces providers of end-to-end encrypted messaging services (iMessage, Signal, \WhatsApp, … but also encrypted email) to check whether users send known CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material). But using AI to scan for new CSAM is encouraged and may be made mandatory later. 

The only known way that works is client-side scanning: hashing the images with a “perceptual hash” (that should be similar for content that looks similar) and comparing the result to a hashed database. Sounds simple but very hard to design.

Shifting the scanning from central to the client seems a minor change but it means that the perceptual hash and the database are implemented on the device and can be reverse engineered. 

Our letter points out 5 main problems. 
1. The technology does not work: it is easy to avoid detection (false negatives) and this is trivial once the perceptual function is known. A more serious problem is a huge number of false positives framing innocent users. Creating deliberate false positives is even easier and will result in a huge number of reports that clog the system.
2. The proposal states that it respects end-to-end encryption, it is obvious that it does not. Scanning happens before encryption and completely undermines it.
3. The measure is indiscriminate: highly intrusive scanning is implemented for every citizen to catch a few bad apples. 
4. It is easy to extend client-side scanning for CSAM to other content, without open democratic control.  EU puts a mass surveillance tool in the hands of dictators.
5. The added complexity makes the apps and devices of all users less secure. By leaking the CSAM database, detection in public environments (that works well now) will be undermined as an unintended side effect.

Conclusion: techno-centric solutions based on surveillance are a very poor option to combat the spread of CSAM. 
Talk to your politicians and tell them to vote no on #chatcontrol. 
If you are a researcher or a scientist, sign the petition at https://lnkd.in/eZmuC2Fq

The European Commission’s proposal to recast the EU CSAM Directive signals a pivotal moment in online child protection. 

Once the recast Directive is adopted, it will establish a firm legal basis for hotlines in the EU to process reports of suspected child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and collaborate with law enforcement and hotlines across borders to remove illegal content online. It also aims to clarify rules around proactive searching, providing Member States the possibility to allow the EU hotlines to examine the source of reported material. This enables hotlines to remove CSAM quicker and in higher volumes, providing critical support for law enforcement, and ensuring the rapid protection of victims.

This fundamental step aligns with INHOPE’s longstanding advocacy for legal recognition of hotlines and represents a significant advancement in the ongoing battle against CSAM online. Read more on how EU hotlines will be impacted 👉

body:
This editorial by child protection organizations in Denmark repeats the same contradictions present in the Chat Control text. It's very unfortunate that organizations doing important and difficult work would believe blindly in a techno-solutionist proposal that creates enormous risks for very little gain in effectiveness against real child abuse.

The editorial repeats the same mistake that Chat Control does not impact end-to-end encryption. The only argument supporting this claim is that it's written in the proposal. It's such an obvious contradiction that Orwell's doublethink pales in comparison: "This ensures that the detection mechanism can access the data in its unencrypted form for effective analysis and action, without compromising the protection provided by end-to-end encryption once the data is transmitted."

The next argument is that scanning will be "limited" to URLs and visual material, like it is a minor inconvenience. It forces a collision between the desire to protect vulnerable people and the fundamental right to private communication.

The core of the issue isn't whether we should fight this horrific material—of course, we should. The EU’s CSAM Law: Totalitarianism Disguised as Protection?

The European Union is proposing yet another intrusive regulation—the so-called CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material) law. At first glance, this legislation, spearheaded by figures like Henna Virkkunen, may seem well-intentioned, aiming to protect children from exploitation. But when examined in the broader context of existing EU measures like the Digital Services Act (DSA), Media Laws, and the proposed Digital ID system, the picture becomes far more alarming.

How the CSAM Law Fits Into the EU’s Framework of Control

The EU already wields significant power over digital platforms and individual freedoms through:

The DSA and DMA: These laws regulate online content and markets, forcing platforms to act as censors under the guise of preventing misinformation or protecting public order.

Media Laws: The EU’s oversight of media content mandates quotas and curbs dissent, often leaving national governments with little room to protect press freedom.

Digital ID: The push for a unified digital identification system aims to centralize citizen data and link all online activity to verified identities.


The CSAM proposal adds yet another layer of mass surveillance to this framework by mandating:

1. Scanning All Digital Communications: This includes private and encrypted messages, effectively ending any semblance of privacy in online interactions.


2. Pervasive Monitoring: Platforms must deploy AI tools to identify and report potential CSAM, even in private conversations.



Why This Is an Unprecedented Threat

When combined, these policies create a chillingly totalitarian system:

No Privacy, Anywhere: The CSAM law ensures that every message you send, even in encrypted apps like Signal or WhatsApp, is monitored. This directly undermines encryption—a critical tool for protecting dissenters, journalists, and whistleblowers.

Universal Surveillance Network: The EU now controls not only what you can say in public (via the DSA and media laws) but also what you can say in private.

Digital Control Over Identity: With Digital ID, your activity can be traced back to you, tying every communication to your verified identity.


The Totalitarian Implications

From an anarcho-capitalist perspective, this is a clear attempt to centralize power under the guise of "protection." The pattern is familiar: governments use fear (whether of misinformation, terrorism, or exploitation) to justify draconian measures.

Weaponizing Fear: By invoking child protection, the EU silences critics who might otherwise oppose such sweeping surveillance.

Erosion of Sovereignty: Member states like Finland are left enforcing policies that strip their citizens of privacy and autonomy.



A Call for Skepticism

Do you trust the EU with this level of control over your life? Should protecting children come at the expense of everyone’s liberty and privacy?

The Danish EU Presidency is pushing for the most radical version yet of the “Chat Control” law. This proposal would mandate the scanning of everyone’s private messages, in the name of 'protecting children online'. 

Let’s be clear: this isn’t about voluntary safety tools. This is about mandatory, mass scanning. This means your device would check your images, videos, and even links before they’re encrypted and sent. Think of it as the post office opening and reading every letter in your living room before you seal the envelope.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫?

End-to-end encryption scrambles a message so only you and the intended recipient can read it. Not the platform, not hackers, not governments. It’s the foundation of secure banking, private conversations, and safe journalism. Weakening it doesn’t just target criminals: it exposes everyone to cyberattacks, identity theft, and surveillance.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐥 𝐢𝐬 𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐞𝐝:

1) Rights violations: this legislation could set a precedent for large-scale scanning of private communications.
2) Security risks: mandatory scanning inevitably weakens encryption, leaving people less secure and more exposed to threats.
3) Experts warn that tools for spotting new CSAM and grooming often make mistakes, with many false alarms and a high risk of wrongly identifying content.
4) False positives: even highly accurate systems would swamp law enforcement with irrelevant reports, pulling resources away from real abuse cases.

There are better ways to protect children. the debate is not a choice between protecting children and preserving privacy, but about ensuring that child-protection measures are effective, proportionate, and respectful of fundamental rights. 

𝐓𝐨 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐫𝐞𝐧 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞, 𝐰𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨:

1) Work with child protection, digital rights, and tech experts to create lawful, targeted, and practical solutions where needed.
2) Prioritise enforcing the Digital Services Act (DSA) so that illegal content is addressed quickly and in a proportionate manner.
3) Delete Child Sexual Abuse Material after investigations, and boost resources for law enforcement and civil groups.

The political reality: some governments now back the Danish push, while others remain undecided. The final decision of the Council could come on 14 October 2025. 

Now is the moment to act. Contact your national government before they take a decision. Tell them: we can protect children without mass surveillance. Weakening encryption is not the answer.

Online child sexual abuse materials (CSAM) and grooming practices (manipulation aimed at exploiting and abusing people), now increasingly targeting younger children, have been proliferating at an alarming rate. In 2023, the more than 36.2 million reports of suspected online child sexual abuse represented a historical peak. Reports of grooming rose by more than 300 % between 2021 and 2023. EU Chat Control Law Proposes Scanning Your Messages - Even Encrypted Ones: 

The European Union is getting closer to passing new rules that would mandate the bulk scanning of digital messages -- including encrypted ones. On Thursday, EU governments will adopt a position on the proposed legislation, which is aimed at detecting child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The vote will determine whether the proposal has enough support to move forward in the EU's law-making process. From a report: The law, first introduced in 2022, would implement an "upload moderation" system that scans all your digital messages, including shared images, videos, and links. Each service required to install this "vetted" monitoring technology must also ask permission to scan your messages. If you don't agree, you won't be able to share images or URLs.

As if this doesn't seem wild enough, the proposed legislation appears to endorse and reject end-to-end encryption at the same time. At first, it highlights how end-to-end encryption "is a necessary means of protecting fundamental rights" but then goes on to say that encrypted messaging services could "inadvertently become secure zones where child sexual abuse material can be shared or disseminated."

EU's Message Scanning Plan Sparks Privacy Concerns

The EU's legislative move to scan private messages for detecting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) has sparked intense debate about online security and privacy. This initiative, particularly stressing under the Belgian presidency, intends to introduce "technologies for upload moderation" within messaging apps, compelling users to allow their messages to be scanned for CSAM. Those who refuse could find themselves restricted to sending only text and audio messages, a significant limitation on the current scope of digital communication.

Meredith Whittaker, president of Signal, vehemently criticizes this approach, accusing EU lawmakers of cloaking a dangerous intrusion into private communication with misleading rhetoric. She points out the inherent conflict between this proposed scanning and the principles of end-to-end encryption (E2EE), suggesting that the former would irrevocably compromise the latter. In parallel, Patrick Breyer, MEP from the Pirate Party, echoes this sentiment, warning that the proposal essentially enforces stringent control over online conversations without altering the essence of the EU Commission's initial proposal.

Despite these criticisms, the draft text of the proposal attempts to reassure by stating it does not intend to ban E2EE or oblige service providers to decrypt messages. It emphasizes that the implementation should not introduce significant cybersecurity risks or enable the inference of communication content. Nevertheless, the controversy centers on the balance between protecting children and preserving the fundamental rights to privacy and secure communication, casting a shadow of concern over the future of digital freedom and safety.

body:
Yes—the EU is considering rules that would put scanning software on your phone.

In Council talks on the CSAM Regulation (COM(2022) 209), the Danish Presidency’s compromise would require device-side checks in encrypted apps at upload (focused on visuals + URLs). If you don’t opt in, you could lose media-sharing in those services. Supporters argue this helps stop child sexual abuse material (CSAM); critics say it undermines encryption in practice and risks false flags, leaks, and mission creep. Relations between journalists-sources-whistleblowers, lawyers-clients, doctors-patients are also under threat. The document has existed since 2022 and has spread a long debate; now, with the Danish presidency, the regulation is back on the agenda.

Since the proposal wants to analyse both existing CSAM and new types of it; as well as do check-ups on E2EE socials, it means that client-side scanning (CSS) is the only solution. CSS practically is checking data before it gets encrypted via sending. This results in the suspicionless inspection of personal data, which European regulators and courts have long deemed an intrusive form of surveillance. Worth noting, that no proven, peer-reviewed method exists to perform CSS on E2EE platforms without creating systemic vulnerabilities. 

A possible scenario where CSS works opens the door to exploitation: researchers have demonstrated that hash matching algorithms can be manipulated – malicious actors could force false matches or evade detection by altering data, potentially framing innocent users or concealing real abuse. If a hacker or hostile government compromises the client-side scanner or the hash database, they might access private data or plant false “alerts”. Taking into account, that algorithms flag summer vacation photos as nudity; taking into account a situation, where a father was flagged as a possible child sex offender when an automated tool used by Google flagged his account and began a 10-month criminal investigation, the probability of the system working flawlessly is small.

And those are just a couple of reasons I've mentioned.
Worth noting, that the document has NOT reached the European Parliament yet.
LV permanent representation's to the EU stance on the document is positive. Yet Latvian MePs are promising to vote against, unless the proposal gets modified.

As Denmark pushes forward on a revived EU “Chat Control” bill mandating scanning of chats—including encrypted ones—it’s not just about child safety. It’s a tectonic shift in how regulators might unravel encryption across Europe. With an October 14, 2025 adoption target, the proposal reignites the privacy vs. security conflict—and it’s critical to compliance, tech strategy, and business risk.

Key Legal Stakes: 
 - End-to-end encryption at risk: Mandatory client-side scans for CSAM would undermine encryption and privacy-by-design principles.
 - Precedent & surveillance creep: The measure, backed by the EU’s ProtectEU strategy, which envisions law enforcement decrypting private data by 2030, could normalize surveillance.
 - Children’s rights as Trojan horse: Noble as child protection is, heavy-handed scanning will likely erode trust, capture irrelevant data, and sweep in non-target populations.

Similar industry resistance shows that once scanning enters law, implications stretch beyond CSAM: data sovereignty, platform liability, AI control, and cross-border compliance.

Why Boards & Privacy Teams Should Care
 - Compliance shift: AI-enabled surveillance could morph into general access mandates, forcing redesigns.
 - Legal risk: Even lawful chat may be captured, raising incident exposure.
 - Strategy: Firms may need to isolate EU-sourced data, update notices, and adopt encrypted enclaves or metadata controls.

With GDPR already policing profiling and transfers, and the EU AI Act looming, Chat Control could join the stack of EU complexities global platforms must navigate.

 - Assess resilience: Can your systems withstand scanning mandates?
 - Map cross-border flows: Where does chat data travel and who holds keys?

Dutch oppose Hungary’s approach to EU child sexual abuse regulation - or total surveillance of every smart device - The Netherlands' government and opposition are both against the latest version of the controversial EU regulation aimed at detecting online child sexual abuse material (CSAM), according to an official position and an open letter published on Tuesday (1 October).

The regulation, aimed at detecting online CSAM, has been criticised for potentially allowing the scanning of private messages on platforms such as WhatsApp or Gmail.

However, the latest compromise text, dated 9 September, limits detection to known material, among other changes. ‘Known’ material refers to content that has already been circulating and detected, in contrast to ‘new’ material that has not yet been identified.

The Hungarian presidency of the Council of the EU shared a partial general approach dated 24 September and seen by Euractiv, that mirrors the 9 September text but reduces the reevaluation period from five years to three for grooming and new CSAM.

Limiting detection to known material could hinder authorities' ability to surveil massive amounts of communications, suggesting the change is likely an attempt to reconcile privacy concerns.

The Netherlands initially supported the proposal to limit detection to 'known' material but withdrew its support in early September, Euractiv reported.

On Tuesday (1 October), Amsterdam officially took a stance against the general approach, despite speculation last week suggesting the country might shift its position in favour of the regulation.

This is also despite the Dutch mostly maintaining that their primary concern lies with combating known CSAM – a focus that aligns with the scope of the latest proposal.

According to various statistics, the Netherlands hosts a significant amount of CSAM.

The Dutch had been considering supporting the proposal, or at least a "silent abstention" that might have weakened the blocking minority, signalling a shift since Friday (27 September), a source close to the matter told Euractiv.

While a change in the Netherlands' stance could have affected the blocking minority in the EU Council, their current position now strengthens it.

If the draft law were to pass in the EU Council, the next stage would be interinstitutional negotiations, called trilogues, between the European Parliament, the Council of the EU, and the Commission to finalise the legislation.

Both the Dutch government and the opposition are against supporting the new partial general approach.

Opposition party GroenLinks-PvdA (Greens/EFA) published an open letter, also on Tuesday, backed by a coalition of national and EU-based private and non-profit organisations, urging the government to vote against the proposal.

🚀  Technology Updates 🚀 
A group of 270 scientists and researchers from different countries are expressing serious concerns about a proposed regulation in the EU. This regulation would require messaging apps to scan for child sexual abuse material (CSAM) using automated detection systems.

The experts believe that this proposal has significant technical flaws and could actually harm the security of communication systems. Even if the detection systems were used, they could produce a large number of false positives, mistakenly flagging innocent messages as CSAM.

EU Chat Control Plan Gains Support Again, Threatens Encryption, mass surveillance, age verification - A controversial European Union proposal dubbed “Chat Control” is regaining momentum, with 19 out of 27 EU member states reportedly backing the measure.

The plan would mandate that messaging platforms, including WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram, must scan every message, photo and video sent by users starting in October, even if end-to-end encryption is in place, popular French tech blogger Korben wrote on Monday.

Denmark reintroduced the proposal on July 1, the first day of its EU Council presidency. France, once opposed, is now in favor, Korben said, citing Patrick Breyer, a former member of the European Parliament for Germany and the European Pirate Party.

Belgium, Hungary, Sweden, Italy and Spain are also in favor, while Germany remains undecided. However, if Berlin joins the majority, a qualified council vote could push the plan through by mid-October, Korben said.

A qualified majority in the EU Council is achieved when two conditions are met. First, at least 55 percent of member states, meaning 15 out of 27, must vote in favor. Second, those countries must represent at least 65% of the EU’s total population.
EU Chat Control bill finds support. Source: Pavol Luptak
Pre-encryption scanning on devices
Instead of weakening encryption, the plan seeks to implement client-side scanning, meaning software embedded in users’ devices that inspects content before it is encrypted. “A bit like if the Post Office came to read all your letters in your living room before you put them in the envelope,” Korben said.

He added that the real target isn’t criminals, who use encrypted or decentralized channels, but ordinary users whose private conversations would now be open to algorithmic scrutiny.

The proposal cites the prevention of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) as its justification. However, it would result in “mass surveillance by means of fully automated real-time surveillance of messaging and chats and the end of privacy of digital correspondence,” Breyer wrote.

Beyond scanning, the package includes mandatory age verification, effectively removing anonymity from messaging platforms. Digital freedom groups are asking citizens to contact their MEPs, sign petitions and push back before the law becomes irreversible.

Source: EU Chat Control Plan Gains Support, Threatens Encryption

Signal, MEPs urge EU Council to drop law that puts a spy on everyone's devices - On Thursday, the EU Council is scheduled to vote on a legislative proposal that would attempt to protect children online by disallowing confidential communication.

The vote had been set for Wednesday but got pushed back .

Known to detractors as Chat Control, the proposal seeks to prevent the online dissemination of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) by requiring internet service providers to scan digital communication – private chats, emails, social media messages, and photos – for unlawful content.

The proposal , recognizing the difficulty of explicitly outlawing encryption, calls for "client-side scanning" or "upload moderation" – analyzing content on people's mobile devices and computers for certain wrongdoing before it gets encrypted and transmitted.

The idea is that algorithms running locally on people's devices will reliably recognize CSAM (and whatever else is deemed sufficiently awful), block it, and/or report it to authorities. This act of automatically policing and reporting people's stuff before it's even had a chance to be securely transferred rather undermines the point of encryption in the first place.

We've been here before. Apple announced plans to implement a client-side scanning scheme back in August 2021, only to face withering criticism from the security community and civil society groups. In late 2021, the iGiant essentially abandoned the idea.

Europe's planned "regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse" is not the only legislative proposal that contemplates client-side scanning as a way to front-run the application of encryption. The US Earn-It Act imagines something similar.

In the UK, the Online Safety Act of 2023 includes a content scanning requirement, though with the government's acknowledgement that enforcement isn't presently feasible. While it does allow telecoms regulator Ofcom to require online platforms to adopt an "accredited technology" to identify unlawful content, there is currently no such technology and it's unclear how accreditation would work.

With the EU proposal vote approaching, opponents of the plan have renewed their calls to shelve the pre-crime surveillance regime.

In an open letter  on Monday, Meredith Whittaker, CEO of Signal, which threatened to withdraw its app from the UK if the Online Safety Act disallowed encryption, reiterated why the EU client-side scanning plan is unworkable and dangerous.

"There is no way to implement such proposals in the context of end-to-end encrypted communications without fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous vulnerability in core infrastructure that would have global implications well beyond Europe," wrote Whittaker.

Hollywood is behind the EU’s new surveillance law? 🤯

Well… not exactly.

We’re talking about the EU Chat Control law, which could force backdoor access to encrypted messages on every phone in Europe. Behind this law is a $24 million lobbying operation run by a Hollywood actor’s tech company.

What is EU Chat Control?

Chat Control (officially the CSAM Regulation) is proposed EU legislation that would mandate client-side scanning of all encrypted messages on platforms like WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, and iMessage.

-The European Commission and Thorn claim it’s about child protection.

-Privacy experts call it a mass surveillance of 450 million Europeans.

So what's the big deal?

-Ashton Kutcher’s tech company Thorn paid a lobbying firm over €600,000 in 2022 for representation in Brussels.

-Another foundation invested $24 million into a lobbying network supporting Chat Control.

-Two Europol officials moved directly to Thorn with no cooling-off period, now lobbying their former colleagues.

-An EU Commissioner wrote directly to Thorn’s CEO, suggesting a long-standing relationship.

-Remember the failed UK surveillance schemes? The same companies are attempting similar setups across Europe.

Why this matters?

-Thorn is U.S.-based, meaning any tech or detection services run on servers outside the EU.

-Scanning private communications, even encrypted ones, opens the door to mass surveillance.

-Many services rely on end-to-end encryption for privacy; the proposal could force backdoors.

-Mission creep: once scanning is in place, it could be expanded beyond CSAM to monitor political dissent, journalism sources, or any content authorities want.

-Legal concerns: questions under EU law and human rights law.

-Technical limitations: AI/automated tools are imperfect, risking false positives or misclassification of innocent content.

For many, this isn’t just about privacy. It’s about building surveillance infrastructure that governments could repurpose. Once client-side scanning exists on every device, authorities could scan for political dissent, whistleblowers, or journalism sources reinforcing the power asymmetry between citizens and the state.

Denmark has set October 14, 2025, as the deadline for Chat Control negotiations and the law could pass with little public scrutiny.

📢 EU 2025 Work Programme: A Step Forward or Just More Red Tape?

The European Commission’s 2025 Work Programme lays out an ambitious vision for competitiveness, sustainability, and simplification. But does it truly cut red tape - or are we still stuck in an endless cycle of new regulations:

🚨 51 new policy initiatives
🚨 123 pending proposals
🔹 11/18 Legislative initiatives are packages or initiatives with simplification objective or significant simplification dimension.
🔹 37 evaluations or fitness checks
🔹 37 proposals for withdrawals
🔹 4 proposals to repeal

✅ Some Steps in the Right Direction:

🔹 Start-up and Scale-up Strategy: Sounds good, but is it enough to tackle Europe’s lack of venture capital and access to risk/growth capital? The CMU was noticeably absent from any mention in the programme, will the 28th regime be able to address some of these problems?

🔹 AILD, SEP, ePrivacy withdrawal: A welcome decision - hopefully the start of rolling back other flawed proposals like CSAM.

🔹 Competitiveness in Focus – The Clean Industrial Deal, Affordable Energy Plan, and Single Market Strategy aim to boost business. But will they truly cut energy costs, speed up permitting, and drive investment?

🔹 Climate Leadership is an economic advantage – The Clean Industrial Deal and 90% emissions reduction by 2040 can drive innovation and investment. Without simpler regulations and a strong CCUS framework, meeting the 50 Mt CO₂ injection target by 2030 is uncertain.

🔹 Commitment to simplification? – The Omnibus simplification packages promise to cut reporting obligations by 25% (35% for SMEs). That’s a positive step, but is it real simplification or just rearranging bureaucracy?

⚠️ Here’s the Problem:

🚨 More new regulations, some withdrawals – Despite the talk of cutting red tape, the legislative pipeline is full, with far more new rules than actual deregulation.

🚨 Energy costs & investment risks – Affordable, reliable energy is key to competitiveness, yet grid upgrades, nuclear, and clean energy projects face regulatory bottlenecks. Can the EU prevent industry from moving elsewhere?

🚨 Digital Networks Act: Opportunity or barrier? – Digital infrastructure is key, but too many past regulations have stifled investment. This must not become another overcomplicated, growth-killing law.

🚨 Will businesses actually feel the difference? – Many of the new simplification initiatives still involve new rules, new compliance measures, and more oversight. 

🚨  European Biotech Act: This would be vital for removing regulatory barriers and boosting biotech innovation and speeding up product approvals. 

💡 The Big Question:

❓ Does this work programme really make it easier to do business in the EU - or just add more layers of compliance? I am doubtful.
Now, it’s on us in the Parliament to ensure the Commission delivers proposals with clear strategic logic that foster growth and innovation - not more barriers.

body:
During its latest plenary, the EDPB adopted an Opinion on the notion of main establishment and on the criteria for the application of the One-Stop-Shop mechanism, following an Art. 64(2) GDPR request by the French Data Protection Authority (DPA). The Opinion clarifies the notion of a controller’s “main establishment” in the EU, in particular for cases where decisions regarding the processing are taken outside the EU. 

In its Opinion, the EDPB considers that a controller’s “place of central administration” in the EU can be considered as a main establishment under Art. 4(16)(a) GDPR only if it takes the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing of personal data and if it has the power to have such decisions implemented. The EDPB further explains that the One-Stop-Shop mechanism can only apply if there is evidence that one of the establishments of the controller in the Union takes decisions on the purposes and means for the relevant processing operations and has the power to have these decisions implemented. This means that, when the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing are taken outside of the EU, there should be no main establishment of the controller in the Union, and therefore the One-Stop-Shop should not apply.

This Opinion is the latest in a series of concrete actions taken by the EDPB following its Vienna Statement on cross-border enforcement, aiming to streamline enforcement and cooperation among DPAs. 
Next, the EDPB adopted a Statement on the legislative developments regarding the Proposal for a Regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse. The Statement follows the EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion on the European Commission’s Proposal for a Regulation and focuses on the latest legislative developments, in particular the position of the European Parliament of November 2023. 

The EDPB stresses the importance to further limit the risk that those orders could affect persons who are unlikely to be involved in child sexual abuse-related crimes. Furthermore, the EDPB regrets that detection orders are not limited to child sexual abuse materials (CSAM) that are already known to authorities, despite the fact that the technologies used to detect new CSAM have proven in the past to have significant error rates.

During the plenary, the EDPB also discussed the scope of the guidance related to the Consent or Pay model. In addition to the upcoming Art. 64 (2) Opinion, which will address the Consent or Pay model in the context of large online platforms, it was agreed that there is a need to consecutively develop Guidelines with a broader scope.

I'd like to raise some awareness on a troubling European legislation proposal that many haven't heard of yet: "Chat Control".

The European Commission is pushing legislation that would mandate scanning of all private digital communications — including encrypted messages, emails, and cloud storage — for child sexual abuse material (CSAM). While the goal is important, the method is deeply troubling: automated mass surveillance of 450 million EU citizens. It doesn't matter if you're using WhatsApp, Telegram, any encrypted messaging service or old school SMS: everything would be exposed.

What I personally find weird about this initiative is that, as general as it is described in the proposals, it could enable client-side scanning—a process in which the content of a message, image, or file is automatically analysed on the sender’s device before it is encrypted and sent. This means that even in services advertised as “end-to-end encrypted” (e.g. Telegram), the privacy of communications would be compromised, because the scan happens in the “clear text” stage when the service provider (or a mandated third party) can inspect the content. 
Introducing such scanning systems effectively creates a backdoor—a permanent point of access that hackers could exploit.

In my view, it would create an immense cyber security burden that no state authority will be able to secure - it would be simply anti-economical, or worse, become a new kind of "black market", or even worse, make personal security issues like child abuse even more dangerous than now.

In summary:
- 📱 Every message, photo, and file scanned—no suspicion required
- 🔓 End-to-end encryption weakened or broken, exposing everyone to security risks
- 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Experts warn this approach is ineffective for child protection and, due to cyber security risks, likely more harmful than useful
- ⚖️ Violates Articles 7 & 8 of the EU Charter on privacy and data protection
- 🎯 AI scanners prone to false positives
- 🧑‍⚖️ Politicians have carved out exemptions for themselves under “professional secrecy”
- 🌍 Sets a dangerous global precedent for authoritarian surveillance

🗓️ Timeline: EU member states must finalize their positions by 12 September 2025, with a decisive vote scheduled for 14 October 20252. This is the final stretch—public pressure now matters more than ever.

🗣️Notable opposition: EDRi has published a collection of 69 opposing voices from EU politicians and member states, tech companies, and child protection experts. 
It also published an open letter signed by over 80 NGOs, almost 500 scientists, and ~90 organizations explaining why this is a deeply troubling initiative which should be stopped.

The proposed "CSAM Regulation," #chatcontrol seeks to fundamentally transform digital communication apps like WhatsApp, iMessage, Instagram, TikTok, and others into tools for mass surveillance. 

The core premise of this regulation is giving up privacy to enable the automatic scanning of all digital communications, including live conversations, photos, and videos, of EU citizens with the aim of identifying potential criminal activity.

However, 100’s of scholars, privacy watchdogs, and even internal lawyers at the Council of the EU have raised substantial concerns about this regulation. Their primary objections revolve around fundamental privacy rights violations and doubts about the effectiveness and reliability of the technology that would be used for its implementation.

One of the major points of contention is the reliance on AI to detect criminal activity within these digital communications. Critics argue that AI systems, while powerful, cannot reliably and accurately identify criminal behavior in the complex and nuanced realm of human communication. As a result, they worry that the system would generate numerous false positives, wrongly labeling innocent citizens as suspects. Moreover, they point out that tech-savvy criminals could easily evade detection by deleting the monitored apps or resorting to the hidden recesses of the dark web.

Critics raise profound concerns about the infringement of fundamental rights, including the right to privacy, freedom of communication, and the presumption of innocence.

As the debate unfolded, it became increasingly apparent that there was insufficient support within the Council of the EU for Commissioner Johansson's proposal. Consequently, the vote on the matter, originally scheduled for Sept 14, was postponed to Thursday, Oct 19.

What adds to the complexity of the situation is a noteworthy move by the Eurocommissioner on Sept 15. On this day, a paid ad campaign was launched on a platform referred to as "X" (formerly Twitter), specifically targeting countries that were reportedly skeptical about the current proposal. This campaign employed emotionally charged imagery, ominous music, and emotional manipulation, suggesting that opposing the bill equated to neglecting the protection of children from abuse. Furthermore, it made misleading claims about widespread support for the proposal among Europeans, based on a survey that selectively highlighted its advantages while omitting the disadvantages.

To sway public opinion, the EU Commission went a step further by utilizing "microtargeting." The EU Commission selectively deployed this strategy to prevent specific groups from seeing these ads. This included individuals concerned about privacy (e.g., those interested in Julian Assange), etc.

In essence, the use of controversial tactics to influence public sentiment within the EU is highly questionable.

The Research surveyed over 30,000 active online child sexual abuse offenders and provides us with a unique set of data that give a clear - albeit appalling- snapshot on the offenders behavioral patterns online. 

Such data is essential and so desperately sought after if we want to ensure that the policy and legislative response is grounded and informed on real life experience and ultimately effective. 

The Research shows the fast race at which CSAM is easily shared on Social Media Platforms and shines light on the distressing accessibility of child sexual abuse material online, predominantly on social media platforms & pornography websites.

❌77% of surveyed offenders encountered CSAM on the open web: especially social media platforms and porn sites;

❌40% of surveyed CSAM offenders attempted to contact a child after viewing CSAM, the majority did so online;

❌CSAM offenders are moving to end-to-end encrypted messaging apps to offend against children without fear of detection;

Unfortunately, the findings of this unique research - albeit shocking - are not surprising to me.

Perpetrators have gone to great lengths to recruit new victims online, and they are always a step ahead, exploiting the vulnerabilities of children online and the loopholes of the social media platforms.

The Internet is flooded with Child Sexual Abuse Imagery and it is fair to say that now more than ever we are facing a public health crisis that puts a huge strain on child victims and it has been facilitated by the accessibility of the tech platforms.

It is clear that the situation has gotten out of hands and we are dealing with multi-faceted challenges that demand urgent and concerted actions! 

Against this backdrop, the most powerful solution is to come up with a robust legislative background that puts victims at the centre and mandates the online communication services providers to embed safety-by-design tools, obliging them to put their house in order and ensure their services are not misused for child sexual abuse purposes.

The EU - with its proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual abuse -has a huge potential to make things right and oblige companies to prioritize children’s safety over profits and to give justice to victims.

Only by detecting and REMOVING all child sexual abuse imagery can we give back victims their agency.

🆕 The EU simplification package and the Commission’s 2025 work programme came out this week. What is (and isn't) in it for IAPP members?

🧱 What it is? 
The ‘Simpler and Faster Europe’ Communication ambitions to:
-reduce bureaucracy: lower administrative costs for all companies by at least 25% and pursue concrete #simplification measure of the entire EU acquis, focusing in 2025 on five ‘omnibus packages’ including on #digitalpolicy. 
-improve how EU rules are made: giving more room to practical implementation in early stages of policymaking and limit secondary legislation;
-improve how rules are implemented: including by increasing stakeholder dialogue and a tougher stance from the Commission on member states that do not implement the rules. 

🧩 How will it happen?
The 2025 Commission work programme is the first piece of the puzzle. 
1. The #Omnibus packages are expected to maximize simplification by addressing interactions between different laws. Among others a Digital package expected in Q4 2025 will:
- review of the #Cybersecurity Act (already planned in the act itself adopted in 2019);
- simplify cybersecurity legislation to avoid duplications of reporting obligations, including with data protection (#GDPR);
- propose a European #Data Union Strategy to simplify “existing data rules” and bring more coherence to data sharing.

2. The Commission wants new #legislation to be “simple, easy to understand and implement, clearly drafted and unambiguous,” and considers implementation and enforcement issues early on during policy drafting. 
One might wonder how that will pan out consider the number of #regulators involved in digital matters alone. Does that mean that EU-level bodies like the EDPB, or advisory entities such as the European Board for Digital Services might be called to play an even bigger role in upstream policymaking?

3. This is notwithstanding several other initiatives already announced/launched, including:
-an Action plan on the cybersecurity of hospitals and healthcare providers (already published);
-an #AI Continent Action Plan.

5. Noteworthy: 
-#ePrivacy proposal is repealed;
-#AIliability proposal is repealed; 
-the #DigitalFairnessAct is not mentioned anywhere. This initiative was under consideration to tackle “unsolved unethical techniques and commercial practices” towards consumers.
-the #CSAM proposal remains on the table despite negotiations in deadlock.

In a dramatic turn of events, Germany has formally blocked the European Union's controversial #ChatControl legislation, effectively killing a vote scheduled for October 14th that would have forced messaging platforms to scan all private communications—including encrypted ones.
Officially called the Child Sexual Abuse Regulation (#CSAR), #ChatControl would have required messaging services like WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram to scan every message, photo, and video on users' devices using AI-powered filters to detect child sexual abuse material (#CSAM). The most alarming aspect: this scanning would occur before messages are encrypted, effectively breaking the fundamental premise of end-to-end #encryption.

#Germany was always a key country. To pass, the regulation needs support representing at least 65% of EU population. Until recently, Germany’s position was uncertain and subject to internal debate. But, in recent days, the German justice minister has publicly rejected the idea of mass, suspicionless scanning of private messages, calling it incompatible with constitutional safeguards in a rule-of-law democracy. As a result, Germany has now blocked the EU’s #ChatControl bill, preventing it from reaching a necessary majority at least for now.

The defeat is crucial for several reasons:
- statistics show high false-positive rates in automated CSAM detection. This means innocent people would have been flagged, and authorities would have accessed countless private communications with no criminal content;
- creating backdoors in encryption doesn't just help law enforcement; it creates vulnerabilities that hackers and hostile nation states could exploit. Government and military communications were notably exempted from the proposal, highlighting that even lawmakers understood the security risks;
- a coalition of over 45,000 European businesses warned the law would destroy user trust and harm Europe's digital sovereignty, placing impossible financial burdens on smaller companies while giving Big Tech an advantage.

While protecting children from online abuse is essential, #ChatControl represents a dangerous approach that conflates surveillance with safety. Mass #surveillance cannot protect children. Real protection requires targeted law enforcement, better platform accountability, education, and resources for identifying actual abusers, and not scanning billions of innocent messages in hopes of finding needles in haystacks.

The October 14th vote will not take place due to lack of majority support. However, privacy advocates warn that "in true European fashion, the same ideas often resurface under different labels after some time".
This victory proves that citizen protest works. Hundreds of cryptography experts, digital rights organizations, and millions of concerned Europeans made their voices heard. But vigilance remains essential. Europe must find the political will to pursue policies that actually work.

EDPB clarifies notion of main establishment and calls on EU legislators to make sure CSAM Regulation respects rights to privacy and data protection: Brussels, 14 February - During its latest plenary, the EDPB adopted an Opinion on the notion of main establishmentand on the criteria for the application of the One-Stop-Shop mechanism, following an Art. 64(2) GDPR request by the French Data Protection Authority (DPA). The Opinion clarifies the notion of a controller’s “main establishment” in the EU, in particular for cases where decisions regarding the processing are taken outside the EU. 


EDPB Chair Anu Talus said: “The notion of main establishment is one of the cornerstones of the One-Stop-Shop. It is key in determining which, if any, DPA is the lead supervisory authority in cross-border data protection cases. The EDPB Opinion sheds further light on the conditions for controllers to access the One-Stop-Shop and provides further guidance for DPAs when determining which DPA is in the lead.” 



In its Opinion, the EDPB considers that a controller’s “place of central administration” in the EU can be considered as a main establishment under Art. 4(16)(a) GDPR only if it takes the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing of personal data and if it has the power to have such decisions implemented. The EDPB further explains that the One-Stop-Shop mechanism can only apply if there is evidence that one of the establishments of the controller in the Union takes decisions on the purposes and means for the relevant processing operations and has the power to have these decisions implemented. This means that, when the decisions on the purposes and means of the processing are taken outside of the EU, there should be no main establishment of the controller in the Union, and therefore the One-Stop-Shop should not apply.


This Opinion is the latest in a series of concrete actions taken by the EDPB following its Vienna Statement on cross-border enforcement, aiming to streamline enforcement and cooperation among DPAs. 


Next, the EDPB adopted a Statement on the legislative developments regarding the Proposal for a Regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse. The Statement follows the EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion on the European Commission’s Proposal for a Regulation and focuses on the latest legislative developments, in particular the position of the European Parliament of November 2023. 


The EDPB welcomes the many improvements proposed by the Parliament, such as exempting end-to-end encrypted communications from detection orders. However, the EDPB regrets that the text proposed by the Parliament does not seem to fully resolve important issues flagged by the EDPB and the EDPS related to general and indiscriminate monitoring of private communications in particular in relation to the issuing of detection orders.

Chat Control 2.0 – Why the Danish Proposal Could End Private Communication in Europe

In October, the EU is set to vote on one of the most controversial digital surveillance laws in its history – the Chat Control proposal.
Originally presented as a tool to combat the spread of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), the newest version, pushed by the Danish EU Presidency, goes far beyond that mission. If passed, it would end the concept of private, secure communication for every citizen in the EU.

What’s in the Proposal?

The Danish plan is more radical than previous drafts:
	•	Mandatory mass scanning of all private messages – including personal chats, emails, and shared images.
	•	Client-side scanning – meaning your device will scan and analyze messages before you send them, effectively breaking secure end-to-end encryption.
	•	Detection of “unknown” content – not just material already flagged as illegal, but anything an AI algorithm thinks might be harmful.
These algorithms are experimental, unreliable, and often prone to false positives.

Government and military accounts, however, will be exempt from this scanning.

Why This is Dangerous

	1.	Loss of True Privacy
Encryption exists to protect your personal data from hackers, criminals, and even governments. Breaking encryption makes everyone less secure – including journalists, activists, businesses, and ordinary people.
	2.	AI Judging Your Conversations
An unaccountable AI system would be scanning not only for known illegal material but also making predictions about “potentially illegal” content.
False accusations and wrongful investigations would become far more likely.
	3.	A Gift to Criminals
Weakening encryption creates backdoors that hackers, hostile states, and cybercriminals can exploit. Ironically, the law could make children and vulnerable people less safe.
	4.	Authoritarian Potential
With government accounts exempt, the law creates a two-tier system: the state is protected, the public is exposed. In the wrong hands, this is the foundation of an Orwellian surveillance regime.


The fight against CSAM is essential, but experts warn that mass scanning is not the solution. Existing tools for targeted investigations, combined with better law enforcement coordination, are far more effective without violating the privacy of millions of innocent people.

The Timeline
	•	September 12 – Governments finalize their positions.
	•	October 14 – Planned vote in the European Parliament.

Once this passes, there is no going back. Technology that can read and flag your private conversations will exist permanently – and can be repurposed for any political or commercial aim.

What You Can Do
	•	Contact your national representatives and MEPs now.
	•	Spread awareness – most citizens have no idea this is about to happen.
	•	Demand that the European Parliament rejects any law that forces mass scanning or breaks encryption.
