🤔 Why is the methodology important for the EU's operational security? 

CSAM supports the #EU’s operational security by outlining the TSOs' requirements to ensure:
🔵 the #ElectricityTransmission system is operated in a coordinated manner; 
🔵 effective system operational planning;
🔵 transparency and reliability of information on #transmission system operation.

🔎 What are the main improvements in the methodology? 

The amendments relate to the implementation of the observability area (i.e. where TSOs implement real-time monitoring and modelling of their systems to maintain #OperationalSecurity).

The main changes include:
🆕 Aligning the observability area reassessment period with that of the external contingency list (i.e., the list of contingencies to be simulated to test the compliance with the operational security limits). This alignment is important to ensure that the operational security analysis is carried out accurately across all timeframes.
🆕 The inclusion of #busbar couplers in the contingency lists and in the TSOs’ Individual #Grid Models (#IGMs), along with a defined timeline for implementation by the TSOs. This update ensures that the #power flows are kept within the operational security limits after a contingency has occurred. 

🐾 What are the next steps?

The #CompetitivenessCompass aims to close the innovation gap, create a roadmap for decarbonisation and competitiveness, reduce excessive dependencies and increase security. 

I fully support its main goals:

👉 Financing: Redirecting EU funds to expand the EIB and EIFs lending capacity via #InvestEU can attract more private investment. 

👉 Internal Market completion: Critical for our growth and to tackle global pressures as well as to reduce strategic dependencies.

👉 Omnibus packages: Pledges to cut red tape at an unprecedented scale through a series of omnibus proposals mainly focuses on green transition now? Surely a digital package likely to follow?

👉 Innovation: A Start-Up and Scale-Up Strategy, AI Initiatives, and a “28th regime” to retain talent in Europe and boost growth alongside proposals on advanced materials, quantum, biotech and robotics show we are focused on the future.

👉 #Climate and #digital transition: Sticking to our 2040 targets. Linking industrial competitiveness with these transitions shows that prosperity, sustainability and technology are inseparable.

👉 Finish the Capital Markets Union. The EU’s fragmented markets block large-scale investment. Member States must address barriers such as pensions, taxation, and insolvency.

What is simplification? Is it about less legislation, outdated rules, or cutting bureaucracy? We can start by removing bad proposals like CSAM, SEP, AI liability, ePrivacy. Focus simplification on high-tech and high-growth sectors. Deregulation isn’t a bad word. ❗️

👉 AI: Gigafactories to train AI models and enable key AI ecosystems throughout the EU is vital to compete. 

Succeed in global (#AI) competition: The U.S. and China are investing heavily in AI, clean tech, and semiconductors. We struggle to attract venture capital and talent at the same rate. ❗️The TechEU investment program and AI gigafactories are promising but may need greater ambition. 

👉 Formulate an EU Talent Retention Strategy. Offer incentives, streamlined visas to keep and attract highly-skilled workers!

Level the playing field for industry: With no complete overhaul of the electricity market, there are changes to price formation and competition but be careful to not undermine market integrity. 👉 Reviewing #CBAM to close loopholes and prevent carbon leakage protects competitiveness in energy-intensive industries. Next? Member States must invest in grids. ☝️

Europe still has many strengths but we cannot downplay the scale and speed of global competition. The Compass provides a framework, but the test is in details, in implementation and in Member States ability to act with unity. 🇪🇺

EU anti-encryption crusaders seek to turn your digital devices into spyware

Not even the most secure VPN could help protect your privacy 🤔 

A few days after EU citizens were called to vote on their next parliamentary representatives, we just have a rough idea of what the upcoming political squad will look like. What is certain, however, is that anti-encryption sentiments are still thriving across the Union.
We already reported the revised proposal to halt the spread of online child sexual abuse material (CSAM) that wants your permission to scan your WhatsApp messages. Now, a leaked 42-point plan puts forward new recommendations on how companies must handle people's online activities, including data retention, access, and interception of all digital services.
The goal is simple: make the digital devices we use every day, from smartphones and smart homes to IoT devices and even cars, legally and technically monitorable at all times by law enforcement bodies. 

According to Jan , CEO at Mullvad—one of the best VPNs around with a privacy-first mandate—all encrypted traffic will no longer be private and secure if the legislation passes. "A VPN won’t help either," he told me. "It would mean total surveillance and that Europe's inhabitants carry state spyware in their pockets."

Data access by design
The intention to implement a so-called "security by design" framework was first shared last year by the High-Level Group (HLG). Created by the European Commission, the group is taking the first steps in what's nicknamed the Going Dark initiative to ensure "the availability of effective law enforcement tools to fight crime and enhance security in the digital age." The process has developed largely behind closed doors so far, with civil society denied a chance to take part.
Encryption is vital to ensure the enjoyment of fundamental rights, like privacy and free speech, but also to allow both citizens and businesses to defend themselves against abuses of information technologies. This was exactly the conclusion of February's judgment published by the European Court of Human Rights which made it illegal to break encryption.

Such a surveillance push from the EU, and ultimately worldwide, authorities is even more worrying when you pair it with the direction Big Tech is headed. Greater data collection is prioritized, which is in stark contrast to GDPR's main concept of data minimization.

EU anti-encryption crusaders seek to turn your digital devices into spyware

Not even the most secure VPN could help protect your privacy 🤔 

A few days after EU citizens were called to vote on their next parliamentary representatives, we just have a rough idea of what the upcoming political squad will look like. What is certain, however, is that anti-encryption sentiments are still thriving across the Union.
We already reported the revised proposal to halt the spread of online child sexual abuse material (CSAM) that wants your permission to scan your WhatsApp messages. Now, a leaked 42-point plan puts forward new recommendations on how companies must handle people's online activities, including data retention, access, and interception of all digital services.
The goal is simple: make the digital devices we use every day, from smartphones and smart homes to IoT devices and even cars, legally and technically monitorable at all times by law enforcement bodies. 

According to Jan Johnson, CEO at Mullvad—one of the best VPNs around with a privacy-first mandate—all encrypted traffic will no longer be private and secure if the legislation passes. "A VPN won’t help either," he told me. "It would mean total surveillance and that Europe's inhabitants carry state spyware in their pockets."

Data access by design
The intention to implement a so-called "security by design" framework was first shared last year by the High-Level Group (HLG). Created by the European Commission, the group is taking the first steps in what's nicknamed the Going Dark initiative to ensure "the availability of effective law enforcement tools to fight crime and enhance security in the digital age." The process has developed largely behind closed doors so far, with civil society denied a chance to take part.
Encryption is vital to ensure the enjoyment of fundamental rights, like privacy and free speech, but also to allow both citizens and businesses to defend themselves against abuses of information technologies. This was exactly the conclusion of February's judgment published by the European Court of Human Rights which made it illegal to break encryption.

Such a surveillance push from the EU, and ultimately worldwide, authorities is even more worrying when you pair it with the direction Big Tech is headed. Greater data collection is prioritized, which is in stark contrast to GDPR's main concept of data minimization.

In a joint open letter, the signatories describe the plan as "technically infeasible" and caution that it would open the door to "unprecedented capabilities for surveillance, control, and censorship."

Their statement arrives just days ahead of a critical European Council meeting on September 12, with a final vote set for October 14 that will determine whether the regulation moves forward.

The proposed law would compel messaging apps, email platforms, cloud services, and even providers of end-to-end encrypted communication to scan all user content automatically. This would apply to texts, images, and videos, whether or not there is any suspicion of wrongdoing.

According to the researchers, such detection systems cannot coexist with secure communication. "On‑device detection, regardless of its technical implementation, inherently undermines the protections that end‑to‑end encryption is designed to guarantee."

By forcing companies to monitor encrypted content, the regulation would introduce security weaknesses that could be exploited by malicious actors and hostile governments.

The scientists also emphasize the inaccuracy of the proposed approach. They argue that large-scale scanning systems produce unacceptable error rates and could generate enormous numbers of false reports.

"Existing research confirms that state‑of‑the‑art detectors would yield unacceptably high false positive and false negative rates, making them unsuitable for large‑scale detection campaigns at the scale of hundreds of millions of users."

Ordinary individuals exchanging private messages could be falsely flagged and subjected to investigation, even in the absence of any illegal behavior.
Proponents of the law have argued that artificial intelligence and machine learning could be used to detect illegal content effectively.

The researchers dispute this claim, writing that "there is no machine‑learning algorithm that can [detect unknown CSAM] without committing a large number of errors … and all known algorithms are fundamentally susceptible to evasion."

In their view, those who intend to spread harmful content could easily sidestep detection using simple technical workarounds, while the broader population would be exposed to widespread and error-prone monitoring.

While several countries, including Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Finland, have already voiced opposition, the outcome now depends on the choices of governments that have not yet committed.

Germany, in particular, could play a decisive role. A vote against or an abstention from Berlin would be enough to block the proposal by helping form the required minority of member states representing at least 35 percent of the EU population.

From Ofcom's post, there will be three phases, with the timing driven by requirements of the Act and relevant secondary legislation:

▶Phase one: Illegal content
First consultation on illegal harms – including child sexual abuse material #CSAM, #terrorist content and #fraud – on 9 November 2023. This will contain proposals for how services can comply with the illegal content #safety duties and draft #codesofpractice.

▶Phase two: #Child safety, #pornography, and protecting women and girls
First consultation, due in December 2023, will set out draft guidance for services that host pornographic content. Further consultations relating to the child safety duties under the Act will follow in Spring 2024; draft guidance on protecting women and girls by Spring 2025.

▶Phase three: Additional duties for categorised services
These duties – including to publish #transparency reports and to deploy user empowerment measures – apply to service which meet certain criteria related to their number of users or #highrisk features of their service. Ofcom advice to the Secretary of State regarding categorisation, and draft guidance on approach to transparency reporting, in Spring 2024.

What about #categories? Subject to the introduction of secondary legislation setting the thresholds for categorisation (i.e. remember it's the Secretary of State who decides on thresholds), Ofcom expects to publish a register of categorised services by the END of 2024.

Further proposals, including a draft code of practice on fraudulent #advertising and #transparency notices will follow in early and mid-2025 respectively, with FINAL codes and guidance published around end 2025.

Still, it's best to start preparing ASAP - 2025 isn't that far off when many changes will be needed including to #policies/ #processes, #technical as well as #organisational, plus changes to #terms and #riskassessments.

Not to mention, the need to consider how best to comply with BOTH the OSA AND the #EU #Digitalservicesact #DSA in a practicable way, for those who are caught by both laws!

body:
Hi network! 

For the question "if EU or U.S. is the biggest CSAM hoster", the best answer would maybe be "we have no idea about it". We do not have any idea of what duplicates are or how long the file has stayed there. 

We could have had but.

Since the current numbers provide no qualitative insight about what is actually going on and where to 'new' (yet not seen) CSAM files are going, the path forward remains also unclear: 

What is really expected for the U.S. - the screening of all file hosters under their jurisdiction because all those CSAM files are something 'they could have seen with a NCMEC plug' or that they start taking the 'new files' indicators finally seriously, because the flood knows no current hash controls? 

We do not know. Alright, NCMEC, IWF and other CSAM hotlines are part of the INHOPE Alliance, which means that hashes are being usually shared. It doesn’t mean they are being analysed - and that is the heart of the story here. 

How hard would have been for an English man to host this very file seen by Big Techs in Rio de Janeiro, where it was also seen? Maybe, the page isn't even in English, payments are only done in reais and through a Brazilian Bank - and the best hypothesis is that this file was downloaded?

On the other hand, if a CSAM file A was only seen in a one-to-one conversation inside Instagram, what the probabilities are that who uploaded it to the Rio de Janeiro server was User A, someone who might have done it easily and an IP Big Techs have? 

This is the heart of Dark Web attribution. Finally. A known attack - correlation, or “I know what you did last summer”.

Amid thousands of reports, where do we go?

Data, we start to see it already - question now is how do we move forward with that, and to start pushing things to a next threat intelligence level.

CSAM Research is not simply a matter of "awareness raising". In fact, this is the very difference between research and advocacy. It is a matter of "what then". Bad enough, but what now: Seeing the facts, what is the proposal here? 

A few ideas - adding also its practical usability. 

Whoever circulates around this file, tell me where else it circulated and all the possible links. Where is the hub? 

A few lines of code, isn’t it? 

Good read! :) 

#csam #trustandsafety #childsafety #threatintelligence #lawenforcement #research

I'm excited to share my Advanced LL.M. thesis (8,5 - A - 1:1) ⚖️ 
This is the third thesis I have authored, and it is the one I'm most proud of thus far. The biggest challenge facing my thesis in its research phase was the lack of research done on the deepfake CSAM of real children, the harmonisation of EU criminal law and analysis of the 2022 Regulatin Proposal. There is quite a lot of research on deepfake pornography created of women, such as AI-generated revenge porn and CSAM, purely AI-generated or created by other means of media, such as Hentai. Many argue that creating deepfake CSAM is a victimless crime, as no real-life abuse has occurred and is simply a utilisation of freedom of speech. However, they fail to recognise the abuse which children face once the content is shared online or through sextortion and blackmail. There is very little research on the intersection of real children used for deepfake CSAM and the compliance of social media with the EU legislation on removing such content from their platforms through the DSA and the 2011 Directive, and what the implementation of the 2022 Regulation Proposal will mean for social media compliance in removing deepfake CSAM.

Despite these limitations, it allowed me to conduct independent analysis and draw original conclusions. I aimed for my thesis to contribute to the conversation on the intersectionality between child safety and AI, highlighting EU legislation and procedural blind spots, and broadening the perspective from only EU member states to a global one, learning from non-member states. 

Through writing a few theses, I have become familiar with my research and writing routine (which includes large quantities of coffee). Despite this, it was the quickest thesis I've had to research and write. Balancing an advanced degree, final exams, and being on the Helga Pedersen Moot Court team with Leiden University, I finished the bulk of it in mid-May to the end of June. Although this has been the most hectic year of my academic career, it has taught me how to juggle multiple projects simultaneously, how to adapt to new working methods, and how to achieve excellent results within a tight timeframe. 

I hope you find it a valuable contribution to the critical discussion on harmonisation of EU criminal law, corporate compliance with legislation safeguarding children, lessons from non-EU states, and the need to adapt procedural processes and legislation to ensure adequate child protection. Going forward, I wish to continue focusing on social media companies’ adherence to EU rules and the safety of children in their interactions with emerging technologies.

Happy reading 🤓

I’m proud to share that my Advanced LL.M. thesis in International & European Human Rights Law recieved a 8.5 (A-1:1)!

Having been inspired by my work on youths freedom of speech online with Amnesty International Norway, my thesis explored social media companies obligations in removing and hindering the dissemination of deepfake child sexual abuse material generated by AI software. I explored the EU’s legislative authority in regulating criminal law, the harmonization of EU criminal law, conducting a doctrinal analysis of the Digital Services Act, the 2022 Regulation Proposal on Child Sexual Abuse, and reflected on both the 2011 Directive on combating child sexual abuse and the 2024 Proposal for a new Directive - all crucial in shaping the regulatory framework for this issue. I concluded that although we are moving in the right direction, there in insufficient protection of children online from deepfake CSAM being generate if the 2022 Regulation Proposal is not adopted in a timely manor to combat the evolving technology. 

This research not only deepened my understanding of the EU’s legislative mechanisms but also broadened my insight into the evolving landscape of child sexual abuse material, especially in the context of AI and deepfake technologies.

A heartfelt thank you to my incredible supervisor, Simona Demková, for your invaluable guidance and support throughout this journey. It’s been a privilege to work with you!

🌟 What an incredible week it has been at the Privacy Symposium in Venice! Meeting with my fabulous business partner Emma Day and spending our days listening to in-depth technical discussions on privacy and data protection and discussing the importance of centring human rights in this discourse, made the 20h trip from Zimbabwe certainly worth it!

💭 A highlight of the trip was my participation in the panel ‘Fighting child sexual abuse material and impact on privacy’, together with Robin Wilton from ISOC and Hans Graux from Timelex. The panel focused on the draft EU CSAM Regulation and its legal, technological and societal challenges. 

🧭 In our discussion, I highlighted the need to consider the impact of the proposal on the functionality and effectiveness of the broader child protection system, and stressed that an increased number of detected images of potentially illegal content does in no way equal the same number of rescued children. To effectively address the issue of technology-facilitated child sexual abuse material, we need to heavily invest in the child protection system and move away from the technosolutionism of the draft Regulation. Further, I highlighted the serious concerns the draft Regulation raises in the context of existing EU law (DSA, e-Commerce Directive, e-Privacy Directive) and its incompatibility with the EU Charter.

Tech Legality is looking forward to continuing these important discussions at the Privacy Symposium 2026!

Hello network, 💙  as you know I’m not a journalist — but I feel this deserves more attention than it’s currently getting. As we return from summer, I want to flag the EU’s renewed proposal known as “𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹” formerly #CSAM. For me it hadn’t really cut through the news fog, yet an important vote is already due this Friday, Sept 12. ⏳ 

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲?
The regulation would make it mandatory for apps like WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage, Telegram, and even email providers to scan all private messages, photos, and videos on your device before they are sent (client-side scanning). 🔍 
The goal is to detect child sexual abuse material — vital in itself — but the method fundamentally alters how end-to-end encryption works by scanning content before it is encrypted. Critics argue this undermines secure private communication. ‼️ 

📄 Current proposal text (EUR-Lex)- https://lnkd.in/gGZ87VFG

Why is this proposal concerning?
𝖯̲𝗋̲𝗂̲𝗏̲𝖺̲𝖼̲𝗒̲ ̲&̲ ̲𝖥̲𝗎̲𝗇̲𝖽̲𝖺̲𝗆̲𝖾̲𝗇̲𝗍̲𝖺̲𝗅̲ ̲𝖱̲𝗂̲𝗀̲𝗁̲𝗍̲𝗌̲:̲ Large-scale scanning risks conflicting with EU Charter rights to privacy and data protection.
𝖥̲𝗋̲𝖾̲𝖾̲𝖽̲𝗈̲𝗆̲ ̲𝗈̲𝖿̲ ̲𝖤̲𝗑̲𝗉̲𝗋̲𝖾̲𝗌̲𝗌̲𝗂̲𝗈̲𝗇̲:̲ Awareness of scanning could foster self-censorship, especially for journalists, whistleblowers, and vulnerable groups.
𝖱̲𝖾̲𝗅̲𝗂̲𝖺̲𝖻̲𝗂̲𝗅̲𝗂̲𝗍̲𝗒̲:̲ Algorithms are error-prone, risking false positives that overwhelm authorities and harm innocents.
𝖢̲𝗒̲𝖻̲𝖾̲𝗋̲𝗌̲𝖾̲𝖼̲𝗎̲𝗋̲𝗂̲𝗍̲𝗒̲:̲ ̲Weakening encryption introduces vulnerabilities for malicious actors to exploit.
𝖯̲𝗋̲𝖾̲𝖼̲𝖾̲𝖽̲𝖾̲𝗇̲𝗍̲:̲ Establishing general scanning in the EU could set a global standard, including in less democratic contexts.

The European Court of Human Rights has previously ruled against broad measures undermining secure communications — raising questions about compatibility.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 voting 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 - ⏩ 
Sept 12: EU Member States state positions.
Oct 14: Council vote (requires 55% of states and 65% of EU’s population).
Current status:
Opposing: Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Finland, Netherlands, Poland, Luxembourg.
Undecided: Germany, Estonia, Slovenia, Greece, Romania.
Supporting: France, Italy, Spain, Ireland, Portugal, Hungary.

🫵  𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼 ⏯️ 
If you feel strongly about this (especially if you live in an undecided country):
1) Reach out to your MEPs or national representatives with respectful but clear messages opposing mandatory scanning. 
2) Sign petitions like to Chat Control or check out https://lnkd.in/gq4cba3T
 (with tools to contact your MEPs).💙

🚨 Urgent Alert: EU's Chat Control Proposal Threatens Our Digital Privacy - And We Can Still Stop It! 🚨

As professionals in privacy tech, we rely on secure communications every day. But a looming EU policy could change that forever. In a must-read post by cryptography expert Tommaso Gagliardoni (link in comments), he dives deep into the technical nightmare of "Chat Control" - the EU's client-side scanning mandate under the Child Sexual Abuse Regulation (CSA Regulation).

𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞'𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐤𝐞𝐲 𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐲: Chat Control requires mandatory software on our devices to scan all messages, photos, and files before they're sent, even in end-to-end encrypted apps like Signal or WhatsApp. It uses AI-driven perceptual hashing and machine learning to detect illegal content like CSAM.

𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘴 𝘸𝘦𝘭𝘭-𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘥? Sure, there are major flaws: closed-source black-box systems prone to false positives/negatives, exploitable vulnerabilities (e.g., model poisoning or extraction), and a setup that's "worse than a backdoor" because it compromises data integrity without directly breaking encryption.

𝘞𝘩𝘺 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘣𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘤𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘥?
𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐜𝐲 𝐄𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: This is mass surveillance on 450M+ EU citizens, violating EU Charter rights to privacy and data protection (Articles 7 & 8). Innocent users could be flagged, leading to unwarranted investigations.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬: It creates systemic weaknesses hackers, criminals, or authoritarian regimes could exploit - think data breaches affecting government comms, IP, or critical infrastructure.

𝐄𝐧𝐝-𝐭𝐨-𝐄𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞: Weakening E2EE for "good reasons" opens doors for all, undermining trust in digital tools we use for business, innovation, and personal life. As Tommaso Gagliardoni warns, there's no "lock only the good guys can open."

𝐆𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭: If passed, it sets a dangerous example worldwide, potentially stifling free expression and secure collaboration.

The vote in the EU Council is set for October 13-14, 2025 - that's just days away! 

But it's not too late to reverse this. Here's what you can do RIGHT NOW:

Excellent line-up of speakers at the High-level panel “Tackling Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation: Global Action to Combat a Global Crime”, that we organized together with the UK government, featuring a powerful keynote address by Her Royal Highness The Duchess of Edinburgh GCVO, Patron of the NSPCC & Plan International UK 

The event was hosted by Hon Caterina Chinnici MEP, Co-Chair of the Integroup on Children’s Rights.

This much needed panel brought together the new EU Commissioner for Internal Affairs & Migration, Magnus Brunner, Jess Phillips MP, UK Minister for Safeguarding and Violence Against Women & Girls, UNODC Alexandra Martins and Mie Kohiyama & Rhiannon-Faye McDonald 

With a new EU Commission in office and less than a year into the 10th legislature of the European Parliament, we have a unique opportunity to renew momentum for passing the EU bill to prevent and combat child sexual abuse.

We must never lose sight of one of the worst epidemics of our time: child sexual exploitation and abuse!

The fast pace at which the new technologies evolve, coupled with the ubiquity of the Internet and its pervasive presence in children’s everyday life, have made it easier for perpetrators to recruit new child victims online, leaving children as easy prey to these heinous crimes.

As HRH The Duchess of Edinburgh recalled in her powerful keynote address, 300 million children have been affected by child sexual exploitation & abuse in the last year.

These appalling figures cannot be ignored by the legislators as though they could just disappear, and they require a global answer. 

The EU Proposal for a Regulation to prevent and combat child sexual exploitation and abuse establishes a robust & solid legal framework that puts victims at the centre through clear obligations to all online communication services providers: 

☑️A mandatory detection system of all instances of child sexual abuse through surgical and targeted detection orders 

☑️ A mandatory removal of all detected CSAM via specific removal orders;


The hungry data-driven business model of the tech platforms also poses unique and unprecedented challenges, that call for the strengthening of preventive measures through statutory duty of care obligations that compel online communication services providers to embed safety-by-design & safety-in-default tools. 

Legislation alone will not be enough, it takes a whole-society approach to bring about a real change in this ecosystem. 

As Alexandra Souza Martins said during the panel, we need to involve new actors - such as financial institutions - which normally shy away from this conversation, whom should instead play an active role in this global fight. 

Huge thanks to colleagues at the UK Home Office Raphaela Thynne MBE Leah Buck Georgia Greaves, and the UK Mission to the EU for the excellent and ongoing cooperation in this global fight.

body:
Wednesday 11 October, I give a presentation for the Commission for Digital Affairs of the Dutch Parliament. 

Also speaking: Jaap-Henk Hoepman, Michel van Eeten, Bert Hubert

Topic: ‘Client Side Scanning’, in the context of the EU’s proposed regulation to fight child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

I will say something along these lines:

Child abuse is a heinous crime, and fighting this crime is hugely important. It is therefore understandable that the European Commission wants to take action. The Commission has proposed a Regulation that aims to curb the sharing of ‘child sexual abuse material' (CSAM). Roughly summarised, the proposal requires communication services such as WhatsApp, Teams, Zoom, and Gmail to detect and block (i) known CSAM, (ii) unknown CSAM, and (iii) grooming. The communication services must report such cases to a newly created EU centre, which will be housed at Europol. 

However, these obligations disproportionately restrict the right to confidentiality of communications and other fundamental rights. First, these obligations require communication services to abandon end-to-end encryption, or apply 'client side scanning'. In both scenarios, the restriction of fundamental rights goes too far. The communications of hundreds of millions of innocent Europeans would be monitored for the authorities. 

Secondly, detecting unknown CSAM material and grooming cases leads to too many 'false positives', and thus to unjustified accusations. Authorities will be overwhelmed and will not be able to check all those false positives. Hence, the requirements will probably be ineffective. This is another reason why the proposal is disproportionate.
